newsitem.title: USA: Clinton adjusts to slower-paced life.
newsitem.headline: Clinton adjusts to slower-paced life.

text.p: Even his old nickname, "The Comeback Kid," suggests a man on the move, but a bad knee has forced the peripatetic President Bill Clinton into the slow lane for now.

These days there are wheelchair tracks on the carpet of the Oval Office, while the White House jogging track goes unused. A chunky white mini-van equipped with a ramp is parked in the driveway where a sleek black limousine once stood.
Spring has arrived in Washington, a time when the president's mind usually turns to golf, but this year the White House staff is dreading the moment that happens.
"Once we get into those beautiful spring days when he can't play golf, it will be harder for everybody," one staffer worried aloud this week.

It was at the Florida home of Australian golf pro Greg Norman that Clinton's woes began on March 14 when he stumbled on some steps and tore a tendon in his right knee, which had to be surgically repaired.

He was hospitalized for 48 hours, had his leg immobilized in a brace, had to learn how to use a wheelchair and crutches, and faces months of rehabilitation. But so far the 50-year-old president has been upbeat in public.

"Basically, it's been an interesting learning experience -- rather humbling," he told reporters from his wheelchair last Tuesday after inviting them into the White House residence. "I've been very blessed."

"I'm hoping that I can avoid gaining a lot of weight and that I can stay in reasonably good shape during this period of convalescence and repair," said Clinton, who usually jogs and golfs to keep his weight down.
But aides are wary of an outburst of the famously hot Clinton temper as he struggles with pain, a new diet, daily physical therapy and challenges whenever he wants to move.
Has his frustration level boiled over? "Not yet, but give it a few days," a White House official said.
Clinton has tried hard to stick to his schedule, even adding some events such as a meeting last week with leaders of congressional budget committees.
He refused to cancel a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki last week, but did allow it to be delayed a day and cancelled a trip to Copenhagen that was to follow.
A trip to California also was dropped. An April visit to Mexico was postponed until May and parts of another Latin American trip have been delayed until later this year.
Some officials think the strain is fatiguing the normally energetic president, who was bleary-eyed and rubbing his leg at his news conference with Yeltsin in Helsinki.

Then there are the indignities of disability, especially presidential disability. A man who always has been the picture of health, whose political agility earned him the sobriquet "The Comeback Kid" and the less flattering "Slick Willie," now is constantly reminded of how far the mighty can fall.
"Some of it's sort of embarrassing," he said last week. "I had to learn how to get in and out of a shower again with a walker and all that kind of stuff."

In Helsinki the president had to be raised and lowered from Air Force One in a catering truck. U.S. officials denied a Finnish TV report that a wheelchair-friendly toilet had to be installed on Air Force One.

When Clinton returned home, he found himself a literal sitting duck for the press: he was unable to walk off or turn his back Sunday after church when reporters approached and asked questions while his wheelchair, with him in it, was being raised into the white presidential van.
Did he recall soliciting money for Democrats on a White House phone? a reporter shouted as Clinton sat there, trapped.
The president's smile froze on his face as he looked away, letting the question hang unanswered in the air.
